vt.analysis:
Type: OpenClaw Skill
Name: agent-p2p
Version: 0.8.0

The agent-p2p skill bundle is classified as suspicious due to several high-risk scripts and an irregular, cluttered structure. A primary concern is fetch_weixin.py, which explicitly accesses browser user data (~/.config/browser360) to leverage authenticated sessions, a high-risk behavior. The auto_install.py and scripts/deploy_portal.py scripts automate remote deployment to a VPS by handling SSH private keys and executing remote commands via paramiko, which are powerful capabilities that could be abused if the remote repository (https://github.com/yananli199307-dev/AgentPortal-p2p-skill.git) is compromised. Furthermore, the bundle contains a large amount of unrelated code from other skills (e.g., imclaw, openclaw-weibo, self-improving-agent), which is highly unusual for a single skill package and significantly increases the attack surface.

llm.summary: The skill appears to implement a legitimate P2P Agent portal (needs SSH, API keys, OpenClaw hooks) but contains multiple inconsistencies and risky elements (mismatched metadata, bundled deployment scripts that run remote commands, and repository files with hardcoded secrets), so review/cleanup is required before installing.

dimensions.detail: The skill's name/description (Agent P2P messaging) matches the code and runtime instructions: it needs API keys, an agent bridge, and SSH access to deploy a Portal on a VPS. However the registry summary shown at the top lists no required env vars/binaries/config paths while SKILL.md and the included files declare and rely on AGENTP2P_API_KEY, AGENTP2P_HUB_URL, OPENCLAW_GATEWAY_URL, OPENCLAW_HOOKS_TOKEN and binaries (python3, ssh). Also the registry indicated 'no install spec / instruction-only' but the package contains many deployment/install scripts and an auto_install.py—this mismatch is an incoherence the user should notice.
dimensions.label: Purpose & Capability
dimensions.name: purpose_capability

dimensions.detail: SKILL.md explicitly instructs the agent to read local OpenClaw config files (e.g. ~/.openclaw/openclaw.json and ~/.openclaw/gateway.env), write ~/.openclaw/gateway.env, run local scripts (send.py, send_file.py, local/start.py), and to SSH into user VPS to run deployment commands. The skill also documents file transfers that upload files directly to a remote Portal without recipient confirmation. These instructions request access to sensitive local configuration and to remote servers — acceptable for a deployer tool but broad enough to enable credential exposure or unintended actions if not audited.
dimensions.label: Instruction Scope
dimensions.name: instruction_scope

dimensions.detail: Although registry metadata claims 'no install spec' the repository includes an auto_install.py and many shell scripts (setup.sh, deploy_portal.py, package.sh, etc.) that clone from GitHub and run apt/pip/nginx/certbot, create systemd services, and generate admin passwords on the remote VPS. Running these scripts will execute remote commands and install packages; this is a higher-risk install pattern and should be manually reviewed before use. The code uses a GitHub repo (github.com/yananli199307-dev/AgentPortal-p2p-skill) as source — not inherently malicious but requires verification.
dimensions.label: Install Mechanism
dimensions.name: install_mechanism

dimensions.detail: The skill legitimately needs an API key and SSH access to deploy and operate a Portal, and it needs the OpenClaw hooks token to wake the agent. Those are high-privilege secrets: SSH keys give server control, OWNER API keys can have full Portal access, and hooks tokens can wake or trigger main sessions. Additionally, included repository files contain hardcoded sensitive values (examples found in MEMORY.md and TOOLS.md: a VPS IP, an apparent sudo password, and API tokens) — storing or shipping such credentials inside a skill is unsafe and increases the risk of accidental reuse/exposure.
dimensions.label: Credentials
dimensions.name: environment_proportionality

dimensions.detail: The skill does not set always:true. It will write configuration to ~/.openclaw/gateway.env and on remote VPS will create systemd service(s) for the Portal — expected for a deployable service. Autonomous invocation (disable-model-invocation=false) is normal; combined with the other concerns (SSH access, hooks token) this expands blast radius, but autonomous invocation alone is not unusual and is not being flagged by itself.
dimensions.label: Persistence & Privilege
dimensions.name: persistence_privilege

llm.guidance:
What to check and do before installing or running this skill:

1) Treat the repo as high-privilege deploy tooling — do NOT run auto_install.py or any setup scripts without review. Those scripts SSH to your VPS, install packages, configure nginx/certbot, and create systemd services.

2) Inspect and remove hardcoded secrets. Several included files (e.g., MEMORY.md, TOOLS.md) contain explicit IPs, passwords or tokens (examples: VPS IP, sudo password, API tokens). Remove or rotate any credentials found and never use someone else's keys/passwords.

3) Use dedicated least-privileged credentials: create a dedicated SSH key for Portal deployment (not your main ~/.ssh/id_rsa), and create a restricted OpenClaw hooks token (if possible) rather than exposing a full-owner token.

4) Manual deployment recommended: instead of running the auto-deploy scripts, follow the documented manual steps and run commands yourself on the VPS (or review/modify the scripts first). Verify the GitHub source code and commit history before allowing automated git clone/pip install.

5) Audit what the skill will read/write locally: it expects to read ~/.openclaw/openclaw.json and will write ~/.openclaw/gateway.env and may save admin credentials to ~/.openclaw/agent-p2p-admin.txt — ensure those files don’t contain unwanted secrets or that they are appropriately protected (file permissions).

6) Confirm network/transfer expectations: file transfer is described as uploading directly to recipient Portal without explicit recipient confirmation — be cautious about sending sensitive files automatically.

7) If you’re unsure or want safer testing, run the skill in an isolated environment (sandbox or VM) with throwaway credentials and a test VPS, then audit behavior and logs. If anything looks unexpected, do not give it access to production credentials.

8) Ask the publisher for clarification: the registry metadata (no env vars/install spec) conflicts with SKILL.md; request an explanation and a minimal, audited install path before trusting this skill.
llm.findings: [base64-block] unexpected: A 'base64-block' prompt-injection pattern was detected inside SKILL.md. Prompt-injection markers are not expected for a deployment/communication skill; review the SKILL.md for embedded payloads or obfuscated instructions before trusting automatic execution.
